steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Elias had tended the Farrow Point Light for thirty-two years before he ever saw a ship in real danger.

The lighthouse stood on a black tooth of rock five miles off the coast, where three tides met and argued. In calm weather the sea stroked the stone like a patient cat; in storms it clawed. The tower rose pale and narrow from the rock, its lantern set in a crown of glass that turned slow as a heartbeat. Elias kept it polished, fueled, and faithful.

He lived alone, unless you counted the foghorn and the gulls. The horn spoke in long, sorrowful blasts on nights when the fog crawled in from the open water, and the gulls laughed at him from the parapet like rude children. Once a month a supply boat came out, when weather allowed. The rest of the time, the world was water and sky and the smiling, indifferent curve of the horizon.

It suited him. On the mainland he had once been a man with a house, a wife, and a son. After the accident on the coastal road, he had walked through his days as if wading in cold syrup, every movement slow and heavy. The lighthouse had been, at the time, an escape disguised as a job. “Someone has to keep the light,” the harbormaster had said. Elias had seized on that sentence, as if duty might anchor him where love had failed.

He kept the light, and in keeping it he learned the language of waves. He knew when a storm was coming by the taste of the air and the way the horizon blurred, by the nervous behavior of the birds. He knew the sound of different hulls beating against the swell, could tell a trawler from a tanker from the low cough of its engines.

At night he read by lamplight in the watch room beneath the lantern—old logbooks, dry manuals, novels the supply captain brought him. The logbooks fascinated him most. They were full of neat, cramped handwriting from men long dead:

“Visibility poor. Lantern at full power. 2 a.m.—heard bell from unseen buoy.”
“Rescued three from overturned dory. Gave blankets, tea. All survived.”

Between the ink lines, Elias began to feel that the lighthouse itself remembered.

The night the ship came was in late autumn, when the sea grows short-tempered. Wind had been swinging all afternoon from south to east, knitting clouds together into a seamless sheet. By sunset the fog was already nosing between the chop, and rain chased it, pattering against the windows. Elias lit the lantern early, climbing the spiral steps with the practiced rhythm of his legs, checking the prisms, the mantle, the rotation mechanism. When the lamp bloomed into white brilliance, the glass room filled with a wet shimmer of light, and the beam swept out, a patient, repeating question to the dark.

Hours passed. The storm arrived in earnest, pressing huge hands against the lighthouse, trying to push it over. The tower groaned, but it had been built by men who understood stone and wind. Rain lashed the lantern glass. Below, the sea hurled itself at the rock.

Around midnight, in a lull between gusts, Elias heard it: three short blasts of a ship’s horn, close and desperate. He froze, every sense straining. Again—three blasts, the last breaking off like a snapped thread.

He grabbed his oilskin coat and ran down to the radio room, boots ringing on iron steps.

“Farrow Point Light to any vessel,” he said into the mic, feeling the old muscles of command return to his voice. “I hear your signal. State your position.”

Static hissed. Wind moaned around the tower. For a moment he thought that was all, and then a voice came back, ragged with panic and bad connection.

“This is the cargo vessel Arden. We’ve lost our navigation. GPS is out. We see your light but—” The rest was drowned in a burst of white noise. “…drift… shoals… can’t get bearings…”

Elias’s hand tightened on the microphone.

“Arden, you’re east of Farrow Point. There are teeth of rock under you. You need to come five degrees starboard and hold that bearing. Do you read?”

Static. Then: “Copy. Five degrees starboard. But she’s… she’s not answering well. We’ve lost most of our power. Can’t see a thing out here.”

He pictured them: a handful of men on a steel island, spray sheeting over the decks, the wind turning their words to mist, the dark pressing like a weight in every direction. Fear, rising like another tide.

“Listen to me,” Elias said. His voice surprised him with its steadiness. “I’m looking at you now.”

He stepped out onto the narrow balcony that circled the lantern, dragging the radio’s cord. Rain slapped his face; the wind tried to tear the words from his mouth.

“I see your mast light to the east. You’re closer than you think. Keep my beam off your port bow. When it swings over you, you’re too far. When you lose sight of it, you’ve gone too far the other way. Do you understand? You chase the edge of my light. Stay in the gray.”

A beat of silence, then the captain’s voice, incredulous. “Chase the edge of your— You’re mad.”

“You called me,” Elias snapped, sharper than he had intended. “You chose my light. Now you listen. The instruments are lying to you tonight. The sea is lying. The only thing telling the truth is this tower. Watch the beam. Follow its border. Trust that it knows the way.”

The wind shrieked at him, as if offended by the claim.

He leaned on the rail, squinting through rain and darkness. Each time the lantern’s beam swung out, it painted the water silver for an instant, throwing up ghostly images of waves and spray. Far off, he saw the faint blur of the Arden’s mast light, jerked and jittered by the roll of her hull.

“Arden, you’re drifting north,” he said. “Correct two degrees starboard. Now. Now.”

In the radio there were shouts, the bark of orders he couldn’t make out. The light shifted minutely. The shadow of the ship fell back toward the path he wanted.

Minutes became a long, stretched thing. Elias forgot the ache in his hands, the wet cold crawling down his collar. He existed only in the rhythm of the turning light, the distant answering movement of the ship, the human voices crackling through the storm.

The sea had taken from him once without asking. It felt, in that moment, as if it were trying to bargain: Give me this one too, and I’ll leave you your quiet.

“No,” Elias said aloud, to the dark and the water and his own memory. “Not tonight.”

The storm built another wall of rain and flung it against the tower. Somewhere far below, waves exploded against rock with the sound of loose cannon. The lantern turned. The ship edged along the invisible curve he had drawn for it with words and light.

“Arden, you’re nearly past the worst,” he said at last. His voice had gone hoarse. “When you see my light dead abeam—beam cutting you in half—you’ll have clear water under your keel. Then you hold that heading for five miles and you’re safe. Do you copy?”

There was a ragged cheer bleeding through the static. Someone said, “We see you—God, we see you—” The captain came back on, sounding like a different man.

“Copy. Dead abeam, then five miles steady. I… Farrow Point, we owe you a drink and more than a drink.”

The wind did not stop. The rain did not soften. But something in the pressure of the night seemed to ease. Elias watched until the Arden’s light became a faint ember and then a doubt and then nothing at all. Only when he was certain the ship was beyond danger did he go back inside, dripping onto the watch room floor.

He set the radio down carefully, as if it were something fragile and alive. On the table lay the open logbook and his pen. For a long moment he stared at the blank line for that night’s entry.

His predecessors had been plain men, their words dry and exact. He had followed their example for years, writing sparse notes: “Routine maintenance. One gull rescued from lantern room. Released.” “Visibility excellent. No incidents.”

He picked up the pen.

“Seas high, visibility poor,” he wrote. The letters were slower than they used to be, but certain. “Guided cargo vessel Arden clear of shoals by light and radio. All hands presumed safe.”

The nib hovered, then moved again, almost of its own accord.

“Tonight remembered why the light is kept.”

He read the sentence twice, surprised to find that it fit.

When he laid the pen down, his hands were shaking. Not from cold; from something looser and warmer moving through his chest, unfreezing places he had once thought permanently locked.

He climbed the spiral once more to the lantern, moving more carefully now, feeling the tiredness in his knees. In the glass room, the great lens turned and turned, casting its measured, unwavering promise out over the restless water.

“Someone has to keep the light,” the harbormaster had said, years ago.

Elias stood with his palm resting lightly on the metal frame, feeling the faint vibration of the gears beneath his skin.

“I’m here,” he said, not loudly, not for anyone else to hear. “I’m here.”

Below, unseen in the dark, the waves clawed and fell away. Out beyond the reach of the beam, the Arden pushed on toward safety, held to her course by the memory of a tower in the storm and a voice in the dark that had said: Trust that it knows the way.

And Farrow Point Light kept turning, steady as breath, waiting for the next ship that might need it.
